paragraphs: Before building something large, an architect surveys the ground and tests it to see whether it can carry the weight. In the same way, the wise legislator does not begin by writing laws that are good in themselves. He begins by examining whether the people they are intended for can accept them. Plato refused to make laws for the Arcadians and the Cyrenaeans, because he knew both peoples were rich and could not tolerate equality. And good laws and bad men existed side by side in Crete, because Minos had imposed discipline on a people already burdened with vice.

A thousand nations have reached greatness on earth without ever being able to endure good laws. Even those that could have endured them could have done so only for a very short stretch of their long history. Most peoples, like most men, are docile only when young; as they grow old they become incorrigible. Once customs are fixed and prejudices deeply rooted, trying to reform them is dangerous and pointless. The people is like a foolish, cowardly patient who raves at the sight of the doctor, and can no longer bear to have anyone touch its faults in order to cure them.

Sometimes, indeed, in the history of States, periods of violence and revolutions do to peoples what certain illnesses do to individuals, turning their heads and making them forget the past. Horror of the past takes the place of forgetfulness, and the State, set on fire by civil wars, is born again, so to speak, from its ashes, and, fresh from the jaws of death, recovers the vigor of youth. Such were Sparta at the time of Lycurgus, Rome after the Tarquins, and, in modern times, Holland and Switzerland after the expulsion of the tyrants.

But such events are rare. They are exceptions, and the cause is always found in the particular constitution of the State concerned. They cannot even happen twice to the same people: a people can free itself while it is still barbarous, but not once the civic impulse has lost its force. Then disorder may destroy it, but revolutions cannot repair it. It needs a master, not a liberator. Free peoples, remember this maxim: “Liberty may be gained, but can never be recovered.”

Youth is not infancy. Nations, like men, have a period of youth, or, we might say, maturity, before which they should not be subjected to laws. But the maturity of a people is not always easy to recognize, and if it is anticipated, the work is spoiled. One people can be disciplined from the start; another cannot, even after ten centuries. Russia will never be truly civilized, because it was civilized too soon. Peter had a talent for imitation, but he lacked true genius, which is creative and makes everything out of nothing. Some of what he did was good, but most of it was out of place. He saw that his people were barbarous, but not that they were unripe for civilization. He wanted to civilize them when they needed only to be hardened. His first wish was to make Germans or Englishmen when he should have been making Russians, and by persuading his subjects that they were what they are not, he kept them from ever becoming what they might have been. A French tutor does the same: he turns his pupil into a child prodigy and then into nothing at all for the rest of his life. The empire of Russia will aspire to conquer Europe, and will itself be conquered. The Tartars, its subjects or neighbors, will become its masters and ours, through a revolution that I regard as inevitable. Indeed, all the kings of Europe are working together to hasten its coming.
